docs.title: adaptiSeq documentation
docs.text:
adaptiSeq is a fast, importable tool for fetching public sequencing data and metadata from GSA, SRA, ENA, DDBJ, and GEO. It accepts any standard accession (Project / Study / BioSample / Sample / Experiment / Run, plus GEO GSE/GSM), resolves it across databases, downloads the sequence files with a segmented, resumable, self-tuning engine, verifies integrity, and optionally converts and merges FASTQ.

adaptiSeq is a tested Python tool with a batch-parallel download path built for the workload real pipelines actually have: lists of accessions, downloaded concurrently, from a script, notebook, or the shell.

Note To use adaptiSeq your system must be connected to the network and able to reach the databases over HTTP, HTTPS, and (optionally) FTP / Aspera.

docs.title: The three things adaptiSeq does
docs.text:
Mode Flag Output Fetch metadata -m ${accession}.metadata.tsv (or .csv + .xlsx for GSA) Download sequence data (default) / -g / -q .sra or *.fastq.gz, md5-verified Convert / merge -q / -e FASTQ (per Run) or merged FASTQ (per Experiment/Sample/Study)

Every Run is md5-checked against the public database; on mismatch adaptiSeq retries up to three rounds, recording successes in success.log and failures in fail.log. The exit status is 1 if any Run could not be delivered and verified.

docs.title: Citation and acknowledgements
docs.text:
A manuscript is in preparation; until it appears, cite the software. Version 0.1.12 is archived on Zenodo as doi:10.5281/zenodo.24062785; the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24062784 always resolves to the latest version. The metadata are in CITATION.cff.

adaptiSeq descends from two earlier tools: iSeq (Chao et al., Bioinformatics, 2024, doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btae641) and FastBioDL (Swargo et al., arXiv:2508.05511). Both are MIT-licensed and their notices are in the repository's LICENSE, under which adaptiSeq is also released.

docs.title: Adaptive controllers
docs.text:
How adaptiSeq decides how many workers to run (or how many connections to hold) during a batch download, so you do not have to pick -j by hand.

Five controllers ship with 0.1.12. Choose one with --controller NAME (or fetch(controller="NAME")); topdown is the default.

Controller What it steers In one sentence topdown (default) the number of active workers (files in flight) explore from the most workers downward to find the knee, commit, then hold and watch bottomup the number of active workers the original gradient optimizer; probes up and down for the whole run greedy the number of active workers every worker runs; backs off by a quarter on HTTP 429/503 and climbs back by a tenth per quiet window budget a per-host connection budget (every worker active) raise while it pays, revert and try a quarter cut when it does not, cut 30 % on pushback knee a per-host connection budget start at 4 connections, double while each doubling pays, settle on the smallest budget that paid, then re-test now and then

ASEQ_ADAPTIVE_MODE (topdown, bottomup, …) selects the controller when neither the flag nor the argument is given; the legacy value climb is an alias for topdown. Implementation: adaptiseq/batch.py, AdaptiveController.

The rest of this page describes topdown, then what the benchmark showed.

docs.title: topdown: the idea in one sentence
docs.text:
Explore top-down to find the knee, commit to it, then hold — re-exploring only if throughput drops in a sustained way.

A worker holds one file; a file is split into up to --max-segments TCP connections. topdown tunes the worker count, i.e. how many files are in flight at once.

flowchart LR
    A[Start: fill meter] --> B[EXPLORE<br/>top-down knee search]
    B --> C[COMMIT<br/>set workers = best]
    C --> D[EXPLOIT<br/>hold + watch passively]
    D -->|sustained drop| B
    D -->|files draining| E[follow cap down]
    E --> D
    D -->|done| F[exit]

docs.title: topdown parameters
docs.text:
Knob Env var Default Meaning probe window --probe-window / ASEQ_PROBE_WINDOW 5 s seconds of throughput averaged per measurement settle ASEQ_TOPDOWN_SETTLE 1.5 s wait after changing the worker count before measuring settle after a step up ASEQ_TOPDOWN_SETTLE_UP 5 s extra wait after raising the count, for the new files to connect drain wait ASEQ_TOPDOWN_DRAIN_S 60 s how long to wait for the files in flight to reach a new count before measuring step-down threshold ASEQ_TOPDOWN_THRESHOLD 0.10 fewer workers must beat more by >10 % to step down re-probe period ASEQ_EXPLOIT_REPROBE_S 20 s how often the exploit phase samples throughput re-explore drop ASEQ_EXPLOIT_REDO 0.35 a >35 % sustained drop below baseline triggers re-explore — (baseline smoothing) — EWMA 0.8/0.2 baseline = 0.8·baseline + 0.2·sample

The pre-rebrand names ASEQ_CLIMB_SETTLE / ASEQ_CLIMB_THRESHOLD are still read as fallbacks when the ASEQ_TOPDOWN_* equivalents are unset. The other controllers read ASEQ_BUDGET_*, ASEQ_KNEE_* and ASEQ_GREEDY_WINDOW (window, start, floor).

docs.title: Phase 1 — EXPLORE (top-down knee search)
docs.text:
Start at the cap (all workers that have files to hold) and step down only while fewer workers is clearly better. On a healthy link "more is better", so the cap wins in about two probes with no slow crawl-up. When high concurrency is being throttled, fewer workers measures faster, so it walks down to the knee.

A count is measured only once the files in flight have come down (or up) to it. If large files do not drain within the drain wait, there is no clean reading at the lower count and the higher one is kept. A step down must also win over a second window (GSA's cut streams make a single window noisy).

cap = min(jobs, files_remaining)
best_w, best_t = cap, measure(cap)
w = cap
while w > 1:
    lower = w // 2
    t = measure(lower)               # None if the pool never reached `lower`
    if t is None: break              # keep the higher count
    if t > best_t * (1 + 0.10):      # looks clearly better ...
        t = (t + measure_again()) / 2    # ... confirm over a second window
        if t > best_t * (1 + 0.10):
            best_w, best_t, w = lower, t, lower
            continue
        break
    if t > best_t:                   # mild gain -> record but stop
        best_w, best_t = lower, t
    break
return best_w

docs.title: Example A — byte-bound workload, no throttling (cap wins fast)
docs.text:
16 large files, cap = 16.

Probe workers measured MB/s decision 1 16 55 best = 16 2 8 30 30 > 55·1.10? no → stop

→ commit 16 workers. Two probes, about 20 s of exploration on a transfer of several minutes.

docs.title: Example B — many connections throttled (steps down to the knee)
docs.text:
Server throttles at high concurrency, cap = 40.

Probe workers measured MB/s decision 1 40 6 best = 40 (throttled) 2 20 21 21 > 6·1.10 = 6.6? yes, confirmed over a second window → best = 20 3 10 19 19 > 21·1.10 = 23? no, and 19 < 21 → stop

→ commit 20 workers. It found the knee (20) and avoided the throttled 40 — without you ever choosing -j 20.

docs.title: Phase 2 — COMMIT + EXPLOIT (hold, watch passively)
docs.text:
Set the pool to best_w and hold. Every reprobe_s (20 s) read the meter without changing the worker count. The first steady reading becomes the committed baseline; later readings update it via EWMA so a transient burst cannot poison it.

set_active(best_w)
committed = 0
low_checks = 0
loop every 20s:
    cap = min(jobs, files_remaining)
    if cap < best_w:            # tail draining -> follow cap down, re-baseline
        best_w = cap; set_active(best_w); committed = 0; continue
    t = meter.recent_average(window)     # passive, no worker change
    if committed == 0: committed = t; continue          # steady baseline
    if t < committed * (1 - 0.35):
        low_checks += 1
        if low_checks >= 2: RE-EXPLORE      # sustained drop -> back to Phase 1
    else:
        low_checks = 0
        committed = 0.8*committed + 0.2*t   # EWMA

docs.title: Example C — sudden speed drop mid-transfer
docs.text:
Committed at 16 workers, baseline ≈ 100 MB/s. The archive starts throttling and throughput collapses.

t (s) passive read vs 65 MB/s (100·0.65) low_checks action 0 100 — 0 baseline set = 100 20 98 ok 0 EWMA → 99.6 40 52 below 1 wait (could be a blip) 60 47 below 2 RE-EXPLORE

Re-explore runs Phase 1 again from the current cap: it measures 16 (still ~50, throttled), 8 (~70 — better, the throttle eases with fewer connections), 4 (~60, not >10 % better) → commit 8. The transfer recovers at 8 workers, mid-flight. The two-consecutive-checks rule (about 40 s) means it reacts to sustained throttling or route changes, not to a single noisy dip.

docs.title: Example D — stable worker = 5, only 3 files remaining
docs.text: best_w = 5, but the batch has drained to 3 files, so cap = min(jobs, 3) = 3 < 5. It follows the drain down to 3 and keeps going — no re-explore is triggered, because the fall in throughput is expected (2 of the 5 workers would have no file to hold anyway). A worker only ever holds one file, so 3 files ⇒ at most 3 useful workers.

docs.title: What the benchmark showed
docs.text:
Choosing the default (controller round 3, build 0.1.12). The five controllers and fixed pools of 20 and 64 workers ran on six lists from ENA, NCBI and GSA, three repetitions each (18 cases). No arm won everywhere. By mean ratio of a case's time to the fastest arm in that case:

Arm Mean ratio to the fastest Mean connections fixed -j 64 1.35 topdown 1.39 (worst case 3.80, an ENA slow spell that timed out four controllers alike) 18.9 greedy 1.41 fixed -j 20 1.55 bottomup 1.62 budget 1.84 13.1 knee 2.15 12.8

topdown was chosen as the default for its average and worst case among the adaptive options. The two controllers that use the fewest connections were the slowest, and remain available (budget, knee) for users who want to load an archive less.

Adaptive versus fixed. On ENA, more connections up to the archive's ceiling nearly always helped, so a fixed pool of 20 beat the adaptive default in most repetitions of the final comparison (by a median 1.6 and 2.0 times on lists of small and large runs on one site, 1.25 and 1.10 on another). The causes seen in the logs: a single failed transport probe that sent a whole list to FTP, range refusals (HTTP 403/416), and a connection limit below what the controller held. The adaptive default needs no value chosen for the list, and across the six controller lists its average was within about 3 % of the best fixed pool; on NCBI extra connections bought nothing and on GSA the best fixed value changed between repetitions.

docs.title: Known limitation
docs.text: On overhead-dominated lists (hundreds of sub-MB files) the small files can all drain during the first probe window, so the controller only ever tunes the big-file tail — it has no lever on the overhead phase. The parallelism itself (-j) is what makes such lists fast.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Notable changes to adaptiSeq. The newest release is first. Versions 0.1.4 to 0.1.11 were internal builds that were never published; their changes are all in 0.1.12 and are listed below under the build that made them.

docs.title: 0.1.13: a Run whose ID starts another ID is no longer skipped
docs.text:
Fixes issue #2, reported by skhakim. success.log and fail.log matched IDs by substring (a port of iSeq's grep -c $ID and sed -i "/$ID/d"), so an ID that is the beginning of another one collided with it: - A Run was skipped as already downloaded. After SRR1234 succeeded, SRR123 was reported as downloaded and never fetched, with exit status 0. - A failure was erased. When SRR123 succeeded, the line of SRR1234 was removed from fail.log. - The sed hint printed for forcing a re-download would also delete the longer ID's line.

An ID now matches an entry only when the entry is that ID or a file name that starts with it and continues with _ or . (SRR123_1.fastq.gz, SRR123.sra), so SRR123 no longer finds SRR1234. The hint, and the examples in the documentation, use sed -i -E '/[[:space:]]ID([^A-Za-z0-9]|$)/d' success.log, which removes the ID and its files and nothing else. success.log is also read once per run and refreshed when the file changes, instead of being read again for every Run (10,000 lookups over a 10,000-line log took 12 s). Nothing in the transfer engine changed; benchmarks of 0.1.12 apply.

docs.title: 0.1.12: first release since 0.1.3
docs.text: This is the build the benchmarks in the accompanying manuscripts ran. In short: - Delivered means verified, and the exit status says so. Each file is checked against the archive's md5 as it lands, and a bad copy is deleted and fetched again inside the pool. A Run that cannot be verified is written to fail.log and the exit status is 1. A Run that ENA cannot serve is fetched from NCBI SRA by default: the fallback is announced, and --no-sra-fallback refuses it (SRA copies cannot be checked against ENA's md5). - Metadata failures are not read as answers. A failed or empty ENA query is retried (up to three minutes of failure, shared by a list) before a Run is declared absent. - Connections stay busy. Files are split into ranges that idle connections take over, the per-host guard reads a refused connect as a ceiling to wait at, and spare connections are used in the tail of a list. GSA runs join the same parallel pool. - Five adaptive controllers (--controller topdown|bottomup|budget|greedy|knee, or fetch(controller=...)); topdown stays the default. See docs/ADAPTIVE_CONTROLLER.md. - GSA and GEO work again after both archives put browser checks on their pages.

docs.title: Details of the 0.1.12 build
docs.text:
• A GSA Run that GSA's run-info table leaves out is no longer skipped with exit 0. The table for a project sometimes comes back without one of its Runs; the Run's metadata CSV then held only a header, nothing was downloaded, and the tool printed "download finished". The run-info query is now retried (4 tries, 2/4/8 s apart); if the Run is still missing, the accession fails, goes to fail.log, and the exit status is non-zero. A header-only CSV left on disk is fetched again instead of trusted.
  • A per-host connection cap lowered by a refused connect or by pushback now climbs back by one connection every 5 s without a new refusal. It used to climb only on a clean new response, and on large files none comes while the cap is held at the open count: in the 0.1.11 controller tournament, runs that met an early refusal from ENA stayed at 25 connections where others reached 50, and GSA tails sank to one connection.
  • When a controller holds files back in the queue and every active worker is busy, the running files may use the spare connection budget (as they already did once the queue was empty). Fixed -j runs are unchanged.
  • topdown (the default controller) measures a worker count only once the files in flight have come down (or up) to it, waits 5 s after a step up for the new files to connect, keeps the higher count when large files do not drain within 60 s, and steps down only when the lower count wins over two windows. It used to read the higher count's throughput right after a step down, and step down on it (many small ENA files: 2-5 workers where 20-50 connections were faster).
  • ENA metadata retries are bounded by time rather than a count: a run waits up to 3 minutes of portal failure before it falls back to SRA, and the 3 minutes are shared by all accessions of a list (one outage costs a list about 3 minutes, not 3 minutes per run). An empty answer that took more than 5 s is retried as a failure, not read as "not in ENA". With 0.1.11 the portal's slow hours sent runs to SRA, whose files cannot be checked against ENA's md5.
  • A segment that runs out of its attempts but made progress continues on a new connection in the same pass; only one that keeps failing without progress ends the pass. On GSA, which cuts streams at any load, each segment that ran out of attempts used to stop its file from splitting for the rest of the pass, and the last minutes of a GSA download ran on a few connections.

docs.title: Details of the internal builds 0.1.4 to 0.1.11
0.1.11 (internal build)
docs.text: • A connect that times out is now handled like a refused connect: while other connections to the host are open it marks the host's connection ceiling and the segment waits for a free slot; with nothing open it is pushback, as before. It used to count as pushback every time, halving the host's connection cap and blocking the host for a backoff. GSA times connects out now and then at any load, so each timeout cut the knee and budget controllers' connection budget by 30 %.

docs.title: 0.1.10 (internal build)
docs.text:
• New controller candidate --controller knee: keeps every worker active and finds the fewest connections that give near-full speed. It starts at 4, doubles while each doubling still earns at least half its proportional gain, settles on the smallest budget that paid, then holds and re-tests a quarter up or down now and then. Server pushback (429/503, refused connects with nothing else open, dropped connections) cuts it by 30 %; responses cut short of their length do not (GSA cuts streams at any load). With -j not given, it may use up to 64 workers, since it limits connections, not workers.
  • A raised connection budget is filled at once: in-flight files split onto all the spare connections in one step instead of one per poll.

docs.title: 0.1.9 (internal build)
docs.text:
• Batch mode: a download that fails but moves its resume point on (the bytes are kept) no longer uses up one of the file's three retries (capped at 20 such passes). Under a storm of cut-short responses, as GSA served at about 40 connections, large files used to run out of retries and fall back to the slow per-Run retry after the batch.
  • A file downloaded on its own (the per-Run retry, single runs) may now split onto spare connections, like a batch file once the queue is empty.
  • Responses cut short of their length are now recorded for the controllers; budget treats 3 or more in one window as distress. budget also keeps adjusting when every file started at once (the queue empty from the start); it only stops in the tail, when its budget is not filled.

docs.title: 0.1.8 (internal build, superseded by 0.1.9)
docs.text:
• New --controller NAME (and fetch(controller=...)) picks the adaptive controller: topdown (the default, unchanged), bottomup (the original gradient optimizer), and two candidates under evaluation: budget, which keeps every worker active and steers a per-host connection budget (raise while it pays, cut when it does not or on server pushback), and greedy, which runs every worker and backs off only on HTTP 429/503. The default will be chosen from a benchmark on every archive adaptiSeq supports.
  • Fix (GSA): GSA's browse page now answers scripts with a browser check and no links, so GSA runs had nothing to download. Links now come from the run-info table GSA's API returns, fetched from download.cncb.ac.cn over HTTPS (-r ftp keeps download.big.ac.cn FTP; Aspera unchanged).
  • GSA in batch mode: GSA runs now join the parallel pool with the other archives (they downloaded one file at a time), with md5 checks in the pool from the project's md5sum.txt.
  • Fix (GEO): GEO's accession page now answers scripts with a reCAPTCHA page, so every GSE/GSM was rejected as invalid. GSE now resolves to its BioProject through NCBI E-utilities (GEO DataSets), GSM to its BioSample (BioSample lists the GSM), within NCBI's request rate; GEO's plain-text record and the page remain as fallbacks.
  • Fix (GSA): the project's md5sum.txt is fetched with retries, and an empty one (left by a refused connection) is fetched again. Previously a failed fetch meant every file of the project was recorded as downloaded without an md5 check. Without an md5 list the file's size must match the run-info table, and the note says the file is not md5-verified.
  • Fix (GSA): after an md5 mismatch the bad file is deleted before the first retry, so the retry downloads again instead of re-checking the same bytes.

docs.title: 0.1.7 (internal build, used for the benchmark)
docs.text: • Fix: a range probe that gets no answer (refused, reset, timed out) is retried, and waits at the host's connection limit like a segment does. Previously it was read as "the server has no ranges" and the whole file went over one connection; when ENA refused a few probes, 1.5 to 2 GB files downloaded single-stream for 15 to 30 min each. A probe that never gets an answer now fails the file (the batch retries it); transport selection still falls back to FTP when HTTPS never answers.

docs.title: 0.1.6 (internal build, used for the benchmark)
docs.text: • Segmented HTTPS keeps a file's connections busy to the end: when a segment finishes, its connection takes over half of the largest remaining piece of the same file, and once the batch queue is empty, unused per-host connection budget splits in-flight files further (up to --max-segments). Previously the last bytes of each file arrived on one connection; on a 16-file, 26 GB list that tail took 15 of 26 minutes.

docs.title: 0.1.5 (internal build, used for the benchmark)
docs.text:
• Fix: an ENA metadata query that fails (HTTP 500, timeout, network error) or comes back with no rows is no longer read as "not in ENA". Previously such a Run went to the SRA fallback, and the converted FASTQ could not be checked against ENA's md5; during an ENA portal outage this hit whole lists. A failed query is now retried like the error body (4 tries, 2/4/8 s apart); an empty answer is retried once, so a Run that is really SRA-only costs one extra query.
  • Batch mode (-j) now says which accessions are downloaded from SRA instead of ENA ("N accession(s) had no usable ENA metadata and will be downloaded from SRA: ..."). Previously that fallback was silent until each Run's verification note.
  • New --no-sra-fallback: a Run with no usable ENA metadata or file fails (exit 1; in a list it goes to fail.log and the rest continue) instead of being fetched from NCBI SRA, so every file that is kept was checked against ENA's md5. A cached SRA runinfo file from an earlier run is queried again on ENA. Cannot be combined with -d sra.
  • Batch mode checks each .fastq.gz against ENA's md5 as soon as it lands. A corrupt transfer is deleted and downloaded again inside the pool, in parallel with the other files, instead of after the batch, one file at a time. The per-Run check reuses the digest rather than hashing the file twice. On a 26 GB, 16-file list with several corrupt transfers, the serial retries had taken 1.5 to 2.5 h of a 2 to 3 h run.
  • Fix: a refused connect while other connections to the same host are open is treated as the host's connection limit (ENA refuses some connects once a client has many open). The per-host cap is held at the number of open connections and the segment waits for a slot. Previously each refusal halved the cap, blocked the host for a backoff, and used up one of the segment's three attempts, so a few refusals could fail a whole file.
  • Batch mode: a file that starts near the end of a batch (or is fetched again after an md5 mismatch) shares the per-host connection budget with the files still to do, so it may use up to --max-segments segments of at least 64 MiB. Previously its split was fixed at size // --segment-size (three for a 1.6 GB file), and the last files of a batch ran on one to three connections. A resumed download keeps the split it started with.

docs.title: 0.1.4 (internal build)
docs.text:
• Fix: -g on a Run with no ENA FASTQ mirror (SRA-only, e.g. SRR1031066) no longer exits with code 1 and a fail.log entry after producing complete FASTQ. The .sra is now validated with vdb-validate, recorded in success.log, and not re-downloaded.
  • Fix: after an MD5 mismatch, the mismatching file is deleted before the first retry, so every retry is a fresh download. Previously the first retry found the full-size file, treated it as already complete, and re-checked the same bytes.
  • Fix: ENA's portal sometimes answers a metadata query with an in-band error (ERROR occurred. Not all results may have been written...). adaptiSeq took that line for a Run, cached it as the accession's .metadata.tsv, and lost the accession. The error body is now retried (4 tries, 2/4/8 s apart, then the SRA fallback) and a cached error body is fetched again.
  • Fix: in an accession list, one accession that cannot be resolved or downloaded no longer stops the rest. It is reported, written to fail.log, and the run continues (exit status 1 at the end). Previously the verification pass after a batch download stopped at that accession, so later Runs were neither md5-checked nor retried. A single accession still raises as before.
  • Fix: resume state left without its data (.part.meta present, .part gone) is discarded instead of resumed. Previously a re-download after an MD5 mismatch could fetch only the segments that state listed as unfinished and leave the rest of the file as zeros; segmented FTP could also report success with no file written. A single-connection download now also clears the resume state of an earlier segmented attempt.
  • Docs: the LICENSE file reproduces the MIT notices of the two earlier tools this code descends from (see Acknowledgements). Comparison table updated for Kingfisher 0.5.0 (Python API, experimental GSA) and pysradb 2.5.1 (--threads).

• Fix: a segmented download whose .part file is missing at finalize (e.g. every segment's connection was refused) now fails cleanly and retries, instead of raising a confusing FileNotFoundError from an unguarded .part rename.

• Fix: the notebook event-loop handling from 0.1.1 now also works when nest_asyncio is active (it previously hung/errored on batch downloads). The API detects a re-entrant loop and drives the coroutine on it directly; plain Jupyter still uses a worker thread. Works with or without nest_asyncio.

• Fix: the Python API (fetch/resolve) now works inside a running asyncio event loop (Jupyter / Google Colab / IPython), where it previously raised asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop. The CLI was unaffected.

docs.title: 0.1.0 (initial release)
docs.text:
• First public release: segmented engine + adaptive batch pool + parallel metadata resolution + adaptive Aspera + Python API.
  • Validated against the real ENA Aspera endpoint with a genuine IBM ascp.
  • Offline test suite (fixtures, engine, batch, adaptive) green; CI on Python 3.10–3.12.

docs.title: Comparison with other tools
docs.text:
adaptiSeq sits among other downloaders for public sequencing data: iSeq, Kingfisher, fastq-dl, fetchngs and pysradb. The first table is the one in the adaptiSeq manuscripts; the cells were read from each tool's help output, source and documentation at the versions shown.

Features compared in the paper (Table I of the manuscript; versions as benchmarked, read from each tool's help output, source and documentation):

Feature adaptiSeq 0.1.12 iSeq 1.9.9 Kingfisher 0.5.0 fastq-dl 4.0.1 fetchngs 1.13.0 pysradb 2.5.1 Accession list in one call ✔ ✔ ✔ – ✔ project Several runs at once ✔ – – – ✔ ✔ Rate-limited parallel resolution ✔ – – – no cap – MD5 check ✔ ✔ optional ✔ ✔ – Resume partial file ✔ ✔ – – per task ✔ Merge runs ✔ ✔ – ✔ – – Python API ✔ – ✔ – – ✔ GSA ✔ ✔† experimental – – – GEO ✔ ✔† – – ✔ ✔ Installation pip, conda conda pip, conda pip, conda Nextflow pip, conda

† iSeq 1.9.9 lists GSA and GEO, but in our tests on 2026-10-19 its GSA run ended with exit status 0 and no data file, and its GEO accession was rejected, after both archives added browser checks to the pages iSeq reads. adaptiSeq reads GSA's run-info table and resolves GEO through NCBI E-utilities instead.

More detail (not in the paper's table):

Software Language Databases Accessions Formats Methods Metadata Several connections per file Adaptive Skip done adaptiSeq Python GSA, SRA, ENA, DDBJ, GEO All fq, fq.gz, sra, bam segmented http(s)/ftp, aspera, wget/axel ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ iSeq Shell GSA†, SRA, ENA, DDBJ, GEO† All fq, fq.gz, sra, bam wget, axel, aspera ✔ ✔ (-p) – ✔ Kingfisher Python SRA, ENA, DDBJ, GSA (experimental) All except GEO fq, fq.gz, sra curl, aria2c, aspera ✔ ✔ (--download-threads) – ✔ fastq-dl Python SRA, ENA, DDBJ All except GSA/GEO fq, fq.gz, sra wget ✔ SRA only (--connections) – ✔ fetchngs Nextflow SRA, ENA, DDBJ, GEO All except GSA fq, fq.gz wget, aspera, prefetch ✔ – – ✔ pysradb Python SRA, ENA, GEO Study, Experiment, GEO fq, fq.gz, sra, bam requests, aspera ✔ – – ✔

Several runs at once = many accessions downloaded in parallel in one run, not one after another · Rate-limited parallel resolution = accession-to-URL lookups run concurrently under a per-endpoint request-rate cap · Adaptive = a controller that tunes the number of concurrent downloads from measured throughput · Python API = an importable library (fetch/resolve/get_metadata), not only a command-line tool. The SRA Toolkit and enaBrowserTools are not compared here.

In this comparison no other tool combines batch download, adaptive concurrency and a Python API. For measurements on a list of 241 runs and one of 8 large runs (speed, completeness and exit status against iSeq, Kingfisher and fastq-dl), see the manuscripts and the benchmark record in the repository's combined-exp-data branch.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Copy-pasteable commands for common tasks. Screenshots are TBD.

docs.title: 1. Everything for a project (data + metadata)
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801

Resolves every Run in the project, downloads each through the segmented engine, and md5-verifies it.

docs.title: 2. Metadata only
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801 -m
adaptiseq -i CRR343031 -m

→ PRJNA211801.metadata.tsv (and for GSA, *.metadata.csv + CRA*.metadata.xlsx).

docs.title: 3. Direct gzip FASTQ
docs.text: adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -g

docs.title: 4. Convert SRA → FASTQ (single-cell friendly)
docs.text: adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -q -t 10

docs.title: 5. Batch download a list, in parallel
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g            # adaptive worker pool (default)
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g -j 8 --no-adaptive   # fixed 8 workers

accessions.txt — one accession per line, databases may be mixed:

SRR7706354
PRJNA480016
CRR311377
GSM7417667

Pick a controller, or require ENA's md5 for every kept file:

adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g --controller budget      # fewest connections
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g --no-sra-fallback        # a Run ENA cannot serve fails

docs.title: 6. Merge an Experiment's Runs
docs.text: adaptiseq -i SRX003906 -g -e ex

docs.title: 7. Aspera (ENA), adaptive pool
docs.text: adaptiseq -i ena_list.txt -a --aspera-efficiency 0.8

docs.title: 8. Force a database / protocol
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -d sra
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354 -g -r https

docs.title: 9. From Python
docs.text:
from adaptiseq import fetch, get_metadata

rows   = get_metadata("SRR7706354")
result = fetch("accessions.txt", outdir="data/", gzip=True, jobs=20, adaptive=True,
               controller="topdown")
print(result.success_ids, result.fail_ids, result.failed)

docs.title: 10. Resume an interrupted run
docs.text:
Just re-run the same command. Completed Runs in success.log are skipped, and partially downloaded files (*.part/*.part.meta) are resumed, not restarted. To force a re-download of one Run:

sed -i -E '/[[:space:]]SRR7706354([^A-Za-z0-9]|$)/d' success.log
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354 -g

docs.title: wget can not be found in your PATH ...
docs.text: adaptiSeq needs wget for metadata/discovery. Install it (e.g. conda install -c conda-forge wget) and re-run. The same message appears for any other required tool the run actually needs.

docs.title: srapath can not be found in your PATH ... on a -g run
docs.text:
A direct ENA *.fastq.gz download needs only wget. You see this only when the run fell back to the SRA path (the file was not on ENA). Install sra-tools:

conda install -c bioconda 'sra-tools>=2.11.0'

adaptiSeq checks srapath / fasterq-dump lazily — only when the SRA fallback is actually taken — so a pure-ENA workflow stays tool-light. (A missing srapath used to be mis-reported as "not available in all databases"; it now gives this clear message instead.)

docs.title: fasterq-dump can not be found ... during conversion
docs.text: The run downloaded a .sra file and needs to convert it (-q, -e, or -g falling back to SRA). Install sra-tools (as above).

docs.title: A download is slow
docs.text:
• Try forcing the SRA database: -d sra (or -d ena).
  • Try a different ENA transport: -r https or -r ftp.
  • For ENA/GSA, try Aspera: -a (needs a real ascp + key).
  • Raise/lower batch concurrency: -j N, or pin it with --no-adaptive.

docs.title: NCBI rate limit / slow metadata for big batches
docs.text:
NCBI E-utilities allows 3 req/s without a key, 10 with one. Export a key:

export NCBI_API_KEY=your_key_here
export NCBI_EMAIL=you@example.com    # optional

docs.title: Aspera (-a) transfers nothing / authentication fails
docs.text:
• Ensure a real IBM ascp is on PATH (a no-op stub passes startup checks but transfers nothing).
  • Ensure a key file exists (adaptiSeq searches the conda env and ~/.aspera).
  • ENA migrated DSA→RSA Aspera keys; the legacy asperaweb_id_dsa.openssh is rejected. adaptiSeq's RSA fallback covers this automatically.

docs.title: A file failed its md5 check
docs.text: adaptiSeq retries up to three rounds, then records the Run in fail.log and deletes the corrupt partial. Re-run the command to retry. To skip checks entirely use -k/--skip-md5 (then re-run without -k to verify later).

docs.title: A Run came from SRA, not ENA. Why?
docs.text: ENA's portal API sometimes fails or returns nothing for a Run, and some Runs are only in NCBI SRA. adaptiSeq retries a failed ENA query for up to about three minutes before it falls back, announces the fallback (N accession(s) had no usable ENA metadata and will be downloaded from SRA), and counts the Run as delivered: its converted FASTQ is validated, but it cannot be compared with ENA's md5. If every kept file must match ENA's md5, add --no-sra-fallback: such a Run then fails, goes to fail.log, and the exit status is 1; re-run later.

docs.title: What does the exit status mean?
docs.text: 0 when every requested Run was delivered; 1 when any Run failed (named in fail.log) or the command could not run. In a list, one failing accession does not stop the rest.

docs.title: Which --controller should I use?
docs.text: Leave the default (topdown) unless you have a reason. greedy runs every worker and backs off on HTTP 429/503; budget and knee hold the fewest connections that give good speed, to load an archive less; bottomup is the original gradient optimizer. See Adaptive controller.

docs.title: How do I re-download something already in success.log?
docs.text:
Remove its line and re-run:

sed -i -E '/[[:space:]]SRR7706354([^A-Za-z0-9]|$)/d' success.log

docs.title: Does -p work with the default engine?
docs.text: No. -p (axel connection count) applies only to --engine classic. The default segmented engine uses --max-segments (per-file ranges) and -j (batch pool) instead.

docs.title: Can I use adaptiSeq as a library?
docs.text: Yes — from adaptiseq import fetch, resolve, get_metadata. See the Python API.

docs.title: Is the output correct?
docs.text: Resolution, metadata, integrity, logs, and merge are covered by a differential test suite that checks adaptiSeq's output against stored reference fixtures. The engine changes only how bytes are transferred, never which bytes are written. 3-file runs (orphan/barcode + _1 + _2) are downloaded correctly (iSeq 1.9.8 did not download them; later iSeq releases do).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: adaptiSeq is a Python package (Python ≥ 3.10) plus a small set of external command-line tools it shells out to.

docs.title: 1. Install with conda (recommended)
docs.text:
The conda package pulls the Python dependencies and every external tool (wget, axel, pigz, coreutils, sra-tools, and aspera-cli for ascp plus its ENA key), so all modes work without further setup:

conda create -n adaptiseq -c conda-forge -c bioconda adaptiseq
conda activate adaptiseq

The package is on Bioconda (version 0.1.12 and later).

Note aspera-cli ships a Linux x86_64 ascp; on other platforms -a is unavailable and the remaining modes work as usual.

docs.title: 2. Install with pip
docs.text:
pip install adaptiseq
adaptiseq --version

pip installs only the Python package. Install the external tools (below) yourself, or use conda.

docs.title: 3. Install from source (development)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/swargo98/adaptiSeq.git
cd adaptiSeq
conda env create -f environment.yml   # external tools + editable install + pytest
conda activate adaptiseq
python -m pytest -q

Without conda, pip install -e '.[test]' gives the editable install and pytest; the external tools must then come from elsewhere.

docs.title: Packaging notes
docs.text:
• recipe/meta.yaml is the recipe that was submitted to bioconda. It builds the released PyPI sdist; its test step runs --version, --help and pip check. CI also builds it and runs the offline test suite shipped in the sdist.
  • environment.yml is the development environment for a checkout.
  • CI builds the recipe and creates the development environment on every push.

docs.title: Python dependencies
docs.text:
Installed automatically by pip:

Package Why aiohttp (≥ 3.8) segmented HTTP(S) engine aioftp (≥ 0.21) native segmented FTP transport numpy (≥ 1.21) gradient adaptive-concurrency controller

docs.title: External command-line tools
docs.text:
adaptiSeq fetches metadata and runs integrity/conversion through a small set of external tools. Which ones you need depends on what you ask for:

Tool Needed for wget metadata / discovery (always) sra-tools (srapath, fasterq-dump, vdb-validate) SRA-fallback resolution, FASTQ conversion, md5/validation pigz gzip compression after conversion (-g/-q) md5sum (coreutils) md5 integrity checks (skipped with -k) axel only the opt-in classic engine with -p IBM ascp (Aspera) only -a

adaptiSeq uses needs-based preflight: a pure ENA *.fastq.gz download needs only wget — sra-tools and the rest are required (with a clear message) only when a run actually takes a path that uses them. See the FAQ for the exact messages and how to resolve them.

docs.title: Verifying the install
docs.text:
adaptiseq --version
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354 -m          # metadata-only smoke test

docs.title: Method details
docs.text:
adaptiSeq fetches every sequence-data byte through a single download seam, so the scheduler and engines change only how bytes arrive and when files are scheduled — never which bytes. Resolution, metadata, integrity, logs, and merge are independent of the transport in use.

An accession list is resolved in parallel under per-archive request limits. Each file becomes a task; workers take tasks, the segmented engine splits each file into byte ranges on several connections, a per-host guard bounds the connections and reacts to refusals, and each finished file is md5-checked inside the pool, with a bad copy going back to the queue. A controller (adaptive or fixed) sets how many files are in flight.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
Engine Flag What it is segmented (default) --engine segmented Resumable, range-based HTTP(S)/FTP downloader (aiohttp/aioftp). Each file is fetched in multiple byte-range connections with atomic .part/.part.meta resume. Runs the batch worker pool and adaptive controller. classic (opt-in) --engine classic The plain-tool path: wget, or axel with -p, plus ascp for -a. No segmentation.

The segmented engine never falls back to classic. A host that cannot serve ranges is downloaded as a single stream inside the segmented engine; --engine classic is a manual choice only.

docs.title: Transport selection (segmented, protocol auto)
docs.text:
For ENA the default is HTTPS-first:

  1. Prefer the HTTPS mirror, confirmed by a cheap per-host range probe.
  2. Else native segmented FTP (REST/RETR via aioftp).
  3. Else a single stream inside the segmented engine.

-r https / -r ftp overrides and is final. A corrupt or zero-byte file is never produced. Per-host transport is cached by kind, not URL (a deliberate fix — a URL cache made every file on a host download the first file's bytes).

docs.title: Download methods summary
docs.text: Method Used for Notes segmented-https ENA/most HTTPS mirrors default; multi-range, resumable segmented-ftp ENA FTP (REST/RETR) when HTTPS ranges unavailable single-stream range-incapable hosts inside the segmented engine; never truncated aspera (ena) ENA, -a adaptive ascp pool (efficiency hysteresis) aspera (gsa) GSA, -a sequential, Huawei-Cloud preferred; best-effort huawei-cloud GSA preferred for GSA even with -a classic wget/axel --engine classic the plain-tool path; axel with -p

docs.title: Concurrency & etiquette
docs.text:
• Per-file: up to --max-segments byte-range connections.
  • Per-file: idle connections take over the remainder of the largest outstanding range of their file (work stealing); a file that starts near the end of a list, or is fetched again after a bad checksum, may use the spare per-host budget.
  • Per-host: one guard for all connections to a host. Its cap defaults to -j × --max-segments (--max-conns-per-host lowers it). A refused connect while other connections are open is read as the host's connection ceiling (wait for a slot, do not back off); HTTP 429/503, or a refusal with nothing open, is pushback (halve the cap, exponential backoff); the cap climbs back by one connection every 5 s without a new refusal. Responses cut short are recorded but not acted on (GSA cuts streams at any load).
  • Per-batch: a worker pool (-j) whose active size an adaptive controller tunes (--adaptive; --controller topdown|bottomup|budget|greedy|knee, topdown by default; see Adaptive controller); workers are gated at file-pickup boundaries.
  • Resolution: parallel (--meta-jobs) under per-endpoint rate limiters (ENA 8 rps, GSA 5, NCBI 3, or 10 with NCBI_API_KEY). A failed or empty ENA answer is retried with backoff and is not read as "not in ENA" until about three minutes of continuous failure, shared by the whole list.
  • Speed: -s/--speed token-bucket cap in MB/s.

docs.title: Integrity
docs.text:
Every Run is md5-checked against the public database (SRA uses md5 + vdb-validate). In a batch, each file is hashed in the worker pool as soon as it lands; a mismatching file is deleted and put back on the queue, so the bad copy is fetched again in parallel with the rest of the list. After the batch a per-Run check confirms every file and retries a Run for up to three rounds, then records the outcome in success.log / fail.log. The exit status is 1 if any Run could not be delivered and verified. -k/--skip-md5 disables the checks.

SRA fallback. When ENA has no usable metadata or file for a Run, adaptiSeq can fetch it from NCBI SRA and convert it. That FASTQ is validated but cannot be compared with ENA's md5, so the fallback is announced and counted as unverified against ENA; --no-sra-fallback makes such a Run fail instead.

docs.title: Usage overview
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accession [options]

-i/--input takes a single accession or a file with one accession per line. adaptiSeq first retrieves the accession's metadata, then downloads each Run it contains, verifies md5, and (optionally) converts/merges.

docs.title: Full option list
docs.text:
Usage:
  adaptiseq -i accession [options]

Required:
  -i, --input     [text|file]   Single accession or a file containing multiple accessions.
                                Note: only one accession per line in the file.

Optional:
  -m, --metadata                Skip the sequencing data downloads and only fetch metadata.
  -g, --gzip                    Download FASTQ files in gzip format directly (*.fastq.gz).
  -q, --fastq                   Convert SRA files to FASTQ format.
  -t, --threads   int           Threads for SRA->FASTQ / compression (default: 8).
  -e, --merge     [ex|sa|st]    Merge fastq files per Experiment, Sample, or Study.
  -d, --database  [ena|sra]     Force database for SRA data (default: auto-detect).
      --no-sra-fallback         Fail a Run that ENA cannot serve instead of fetching it from SRA,
                                so every kept file can be checked against ENA's md5.
  -p, --parallel  int           axel connection count (classic engine only), e.g. -p 10.
  -a, --aspera                  Use Aspera (ascp); GSA/ENA only.
  -s, --speed     int           Download speed limit (MB/s) (default: 1000).
  -k, --skip-md5                Skip the md5 check for downloaded files.
  -r, --protocol  [ftp|https]   ENA transport (default: auto, HTTPS-first).
  -Q, --quiet                   Suppress download progress bars.
  -o, --output    text          Output directory (created if missing; default: cwd).

Engine / batch / adaptive:
  --engine        [segmented|classic]   Download engine (default: segmented).
  --segment-size  int           Target segment size in MB (default: 512).
  --max-segments  int           Max connections per file (default: 8).
  --max-conns-per-host int      Cap on connections to one host (default: auto = -j x --max-segments;
                                the circuit breaker still lowers it on 429/503).
  -j, --jobs      int           Max worker-pool size for batch download (default: 20).
  --adaptive / --no-adaptive    Adaptive concurrency (default: on); --no-adaptive runs all -j workers.
  --controller    name          Adaptive controller: topdown (default), bottomup, budget, greedy, knee.
  --probe-window  int           Adaptive probe window in seconds (default: 5).
  --cc-penalty    float         Worker-cost penalty K in score=throughput/K**workers (default: 1.01).
  --meta-jobs     int           Parallelism for metadata/URL resolution (default: 3).
  --aspera-efficiency float     Keep an extra ascp worker only above this efficiency (default: 0.70).

  -h, --help                    Show help.
  -v, --version                 Show version.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Downloading sequence data — the default download path, -g, -q, -d, -r, -p
  • Fetching metadata — -m, and what files you get per database
  • Merging FASTQ — -e ex|sa|st
  • Batch & adaptive download — accession lists, -j, --adaptive, --meta-jobs
  • Aspera — -a and the adaptive ascp pool
  • Python API — fetch, resolve, get_metadata

docs.title: Logs and re-runs
docs.text:
File Contents success.log Runs downloaded and verified fail.log Runs that failed after 3 retry rounds

Exit status: 0 when every requested Run was delivered, 1 when any Run failed (named in fail.log) or the command could not run. A Run fetched from NCBI SRA because ENA could not serve it is announced and counts as delivered, unless --no-sra-fallback is given, in which case it fails.

A Run already in success.log is skipped on re-run; remove its line (e.g. sed -i -E '/[[:space:]]SRR7706354([^A-Za-z0-9]|$)/d' success.log) to force a re-download. Partial files left by the segmented engine (*.part, *.part.meta) are resumed, not restarted.

docs.title: Aspera (-a)
docs.text:
Use IBM Aspera (ascp) for high-speed transfer.

adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801 -a -g

Aspera is opt-in and supported for GSA / ENA only — the NCBI SRA database does not offer Aspera, so adaptiSeq downloads SRA files over HTTPS instead.

docs.title: Adaptive parallel Aspera (ENA)
docs.text:
ascp cannot pause/resume mid-file, so the gradient batch controller (which pauses and re-queues files) does not apply. Instead, with -a adaptiSeq runs a parallel ascp pool gated at file-pickup boundaries, tuned by an additive-increase + efficiency-hysteresis controller:

  1. Measure single-worker throughput (baseline).
  2. Each interval, tentatively add one worker.
  3. Keep it only if aggregate throughput reaches at least --aspera-efficiency (default 0.70) of workers × baseline; otherwise drop it and hold (no flapping).

Because ascp writes bytes out-of-process, throughput is measured by sampling output-directory growth.

adaptiseq -i ena_list.txt -a --aspera-efficiency 0.8

This path is validated against the real ENA Aspera endpoint with a genuine IBM ascp: single-file and multi-file batches transfer and pass md5, and the controller correctly backs off to one session when ENA throttles a second concurrent ascp.

docs.title: GSA Aspera
docs.text: GSA Aspera is supported on a sequential, best-effort basis. The Huawei-Cloud preference rule: when a Huawei-Cloud link is available adaptiSeq prefers it (faster/more stable) even with -a, so -a is still recommended for GSA as a fast fallback. GSA Aspera has not yet been validated against the live endpoint here.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Note 1 -a requires a real IBM ascp on PATH. A no-op stub will pass startup checks but transfer nothing.

Note 2 Aspera needs a key file. adaptiSeq searches the conda environment and ~/.aspera automatically. ENA migrated its Aspera auth from DSA to RSA keys; the legacy asperaweb_id_dsa.openssh is now rejected, but adaptiSeq's RSA fallback covers it.

docs.title: Speed cap
docs.text: -s/--speed (MB/s) applies to Aspera as well as the HTTP(S)/FTP engines.

docs.title: Batch & adaptive download
docs.text:
adaptiSeq is built for the workload real pipelines have: lists of accessions, downloaded concurrently. Pass a file (one accession per line) — mixed SRA/ENA/GSA is fine:

adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g

docs.title: How a batch runs
docs.text:
For accessions on the default segmented engine, adaptiSeq runs a two-phase batch:

  1. Parallel resolution (--meta-jobs, default 3) — resolves accession → URLs and checksums for the whole list concurrently, each archive endpoint behind its own rate limiter (ENA 8 requests/s, GSA 5, NCBI 3, or 10 with NCBI_API_KEY). A failed or empty ENA answer is retried with backoff and is not read as "not in ENA" until about three minutes of continuous failure, a budget shared by the whole list. Only then does a Run fall back to NCBI SRA — and the fallback is announced (N accession(s) had no usable ENA metadata and will be downloaded from SRA: ...). Use --no-sra-fallback to refuse it.
  2. Adaptive download pool (-j, default 20) — a single-process asyncio worker pool pulls the resolved files; each file is fetched by the segmented engine in byte ranges on several connections, and idle connections take over the remainder of the largest outstanding range, so connections stay busy until the last byte.

Per-file semantics: skip-if-in-success.log; each file is md5-checked in the pool as soon as it lands, and a corrupt copy is deleted and fetched again in parallel with the rest of the list (not after the batch); retry up to 3 rounds; failures go to fail.log while the rest of the list continues; the overall exit status is 1 if any Run could not be delivered and verified.

GSA accessions join the same pool (their links come from GSA's run-info table). The sequential path is used for --engine classic, for -m (metadata only), and for GSA with Aspera.

Note Resolution finishes for the whole batch before downloading starts; the two phases do not currently overlap. (The internal resolve_all exposes an on_task hook for future producer/consumer streaming.)

docs.title: -j, --jobs — worker-pool size
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g -j 8

Maximum number of files downloading at once (default 20). With --adaptive (the default), this is the ceiling; the controller chooses how many of these workers are actually active. (The knee controller limits connections, not workers, and may use up to 64 workers when -j is not given.)

docs.title: --adaptive / --no-adaptive
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g                 # adaptive (default)
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g --no-adaptive   # fixed: all -j workers, no probing

An adaptive controller measures achieved throughput and tunes how many workers are active, backing off when extra workers stop paying for themselves (so you neither under-utilise the link nor hammer the server). Controllers gate workers at file-pickup boundaries — they never cancel an in-flight download, which would risk corruption — so they change how many files download at once, not which bytes are written.

docs.title: --controller — which adaptive controller
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g --controller budget
Controller What it does Use it when topdown (default) starts at the most workers that have files to hold and steps down only when fewer is clearly faster; then watches the rate passively and searches again after a sustained drop you want no tuning bottomup the original gradient optimizer: keeps probing up and down for comparison greedy every worker active; backs off only on HTTP 429/503 the archive does not push back and you want -j behaviour with a safety valve budget every worker active; steers a per-host connection budget: raises while it pays, cuts when it does not or on pushback you want the fewest connections for good speed (loads the archive least) knee every worker active; starts at 4 connections and doubles while each doubling pays, then settles on the smallest budget that paid you want the fewest connections for near-full speed

The two that limit connections (budget and knee) used the fewest connections in our benchmark (about 13 on average, against 19 for topdown) and were slower on average than holding many connections; they stay available for users who want to load an archive less. How each works and what the benchmark showed: Adaptive controller. From Python: fetch(..., controller="knee"). The environment variable ASEQ_ADAPTIVE_MODE sets the controller when neither the flag nor the argument is given.

Tuning knobs (topdown and bottomup):

Flag Meaning Default --probe-window seconds per probe before re-measuring 5 --cc-penalty worker-cost penalty K in score = throughput / K**workers 1.01

The chosen trajectory (e.g. 1w@…→2w@…) is logged at the end of the run.

Honesty note In our benchmark on ENA, a fixed pool (--no-adaptive -j 20) was usually faster than the adaptive default (on one site the default took a median 1.6 and 2.0 times as long on a list of small runs and of large runs, on a second site 1.25 and 1.10), because more connections up to the archive's ceiling nearly always helped there. The adaptive default needs no value chosen for the list and is within about 3 % of the best fixed pool on lists from ENA, NCBI and GSA taken together; on NCBI extra connections bought nothing, and on GSA the best fixed value changed from run to run.

docs.title: --meta-jobs — resolution parallelism
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i big_list.txt -g --meta-jobs 5

How many accessions resolve concurrently (default 3). Bounded by per-endpoint rate limiters, not by pool size; NCBI E-utilities is held to 3 req/s (10 with NCBI_API_KEY).

docs.title: Segmented-engine knobs
docs.text:
Flag Meaning Default --segment-size target byte-range segment size (MB) 512 --max-segments max concurrent connections per file 8 --max-conns-per-host cap on connections to any one host auto (-j × --max-segments)

A file is split into one range per --segment-size, at most --max-segments (a file near the end of the list, or one fetched again after a bad checksum, may use more of the spare budget). Set --max-conns-per-host lower to be gentler on a host. The per-host guard also reacts to the archive: a refused connect while other connections are open is read as the host's connection ceiling (it waits for a slot instead of backing off), HTTP 429/503 halves the cap with exponential backoff, and the cap climbs back by one connection every 5 s without a new refusal. Together these keep adaptiSeq a polite client even at high concurrency.

docs.title: Downloading sequence data
docs.text:
By default adaptiseq -i <accession> resolves the accession, downloads every Run it contains through the segmented engine, and md5-verifies each file.

adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801          # all Runs in a project
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354           # a single Run
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt       # a file of accessions (batch; see batch.md)

For each Run, adaptiSeq downloads, checks the md5 against the public database, and on mismatch retries up to three rounds before recording the result in success.log / fail.log.

docs.title: -g, --gzip — direct *.fastq.gz
docs.text:
Download FASTQ directly in gzip format.

adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -g

For GSA accessions most data is already gzip, so -g is effectively always on. For SRA/ENA/DDBJ/GEO, adaptiSeq first tries ENA's *.fastq.gz mirror; if that is unavailable it falls back to downloading the .sra file and converting it with fasterq-dump + pigz.

Note A pure ENA *.fastq.gz download needs only wget (plus pigz for any conversion). sra-tools is required only if the SRA fallback actually triggers — adaptiSeq then prints a clear "install sra-tools" message rather than failing obscurely.

docs.title: -q, --fastq — convert SRA to FASTQ
docs.text:
After downloading the .sra file, decompose it into uncompressed FASTQ with fasterq-dump.

adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -q
adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -q -t 10      # 10 conversion threads

Note -q is particularly useful for single-cell data: it can decompose a run into I1/R1/R2/R3, whereas a direct -g download may yield only R1/R3. Used together, -q -g downloads the .sra, converts it, then gzips the result.

docs.title: -t, --threads
docs.text:
Threads for SRA→FASTQ conversion and gzip compression (default 8).

adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -q -t 10

More is not always better — fasterq-dump is IO-heavy, and too many threads raise CPU/IO load. A ceiling around 15 is a sensible default.

docs.title: -d, --database — force ENA or SRA
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i SRR1178105 -d sra

By default adaptiSeq auto-detects the best database, so -d is usually unnecessary. Force -d sra when ENA is slow for a given file.

Note If a file is not in ENA, adaptiSeq switches to SRA automatically even with -d ena.

docs.title: --no-sra-fallback — ENA or nothing
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i accessions.txt -g --no-sra-fallback

Fail a Run instead of fetching it from SRA when ENA has no usable metadata or file for it (after the usual retries). FASTQ converted from an SRA file cannot be checked against ENA's md5, so use this when every kept file must be md5-verified, e.g. in a pipeline or a benchmark. adaptiSeq exits 1; in a list, the failed accessions go to fail.log and the rest continue. Re-run them later, or without the flag to accept SRA. Cannot be combined with -d sra.

docs.title: -r, --protocol — ENA transport
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354 -g -r https

For the segmented engine, ENA transport defaults to auto (HTTPS-first): it prefers the HTTPS mirror (confirmed by a cheap per-host range probe), then native segmented FTP, then a single stream inside the segmented engine. Pass -r https or -r ftp to force one.

docs.title: -p, --parallel — classic-engine parallelism
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801 --engine classic -p 10

-p sets the axel connection count and applies only to the opt-in classic engine (--engine classic). The default segmented engine already fetches each file in multiple byte-range connections (--max-segments) and runs a batch worker pool (-j), so -p is not needed there. See Method details.

docs.title: -s, --speed — speed cap
docs.text:
adaptiseq -i SRR7706354 -g -s 50      # cap at 50 MB/s

Token-bucket rate limit in MB/s (default 1000), applied by the engine.

docs.title: -k, --skip-md5
docs.text: Skip md5/vdb-validate integrity checks. Remove -k and re-run to verify later.

docs.title: -Q, --quiet
docs.text: Suppress the live progress bar and non-essential messages — cleaner logs for batch/CI use.

docs.title: Merging FASTQ (-e)
docs.text:
Merge the FASTQ files of multiple Runs into one file per Experiment (ex), Sample (sa), or Study (st).

adaptiseq -i SRX003906 -g -e ex

Most Experiments contain a single Run, but some span several (e.g. SRX003906, CRX020217). -e merges them in a consistent order so paired-end _1/_2 files stay aligned.

  • -e ex — merge all FASTQ of the same Experiment. Accepts ERX, DRX, SRX, CRX.
  • -e sa — merge all FASTQ of the same Sample. Accepts ERS, DRS, SRS, SAMC, GSM.
  • -e st — merge all FASTQ of the same Study. Accepts ERP, DRP, SRP, CRA.

Output:

  • single-end → SRX*.fastq.gz
  • paired-end → SRX*_1.fastq.gz and SRX*_2.fastq.gz

Note 1 -e cannot be used when the input accession is a Run ID. adaptiSeq merges gzip-compressed and uncompressed FASTQ, but not BAM or tar.gz files.

Note 2 When an Experiment has one Run and the Run's files share its prefix, adaptiSeq renames them directly to SRX*_1.fastq.gz / SRX*_2.fastq.gz. When a Run's files use different prefixes (e.g. CRX006713/CRR007192), they are renamed as SRX*_<original_filename>.

Note 3 Merge logic is deterministic — the same inputs produce the same merged bytes. adaptiSeq's engine changes only how the per-Run files are fetched, never their contents.

docs.title: Fetching metadata (-m)
docs.text:
Download only the sample metadata for an accession and skip the sequence data.

adaptiseq -i PRJNA211801 -m
adaptiseq -i CRR343031 -m

Metadata is always fetched (with or without -m) because it drives resolution; if metadata cannot be retrieved, adaptiSeq stops before downloading. The metadata bytes are pulled with wget, so the files are exactly what the archive serves.

docs.title: SRA / ENA / DDBJ / GEO
docs.text:
adaptiSeq first queries ENA. If sample information is available it downloads metadata in TSV format via the ENA Portal API (typically ~191 columns), saved as ${accession}.metadata.tsv.

If ENA has no record yet (common for very recently released SRA data), adaptiSeq falls back to the SRA Database Backend, downloading CSV (~30 columns) and converting it to TSV for consistency.

docs.title: GSA
docs.text: For GSA accessions, adaptiSeq uses GSA's getRunInfo interface to download CSV metadata (~25 columns), saved as ${accession}.metadata.csv, and the exportExcelFile interface for the parent Project's XLSX (sheets Sample, Experiment, Run), saved as CRA*.metadata.xlsx.

docs.title: In the Python API
docs.text:
get_metadata returns the parsed rows as a list of dicts (and writes the same files):

from adaptiseq import get_metadata

rows = get_metadata("SRR7706354")          # ENA/SRA -> list[dict] of TSV columns
rows = get_metadata("CRR311377")           # GSA     -> list[dict] of CSV columns

See the Python API page.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Database Files SRA / ENA / DDBJ / GEO ${accession}.metadata.tsv GSA ${accession}.metadata.csv, CRA*.metadata.xlsx

Note NCBI E-utilities is rate-limited to 3 req/s without a key and 10 req/s with one. Set NCBI_API_KEY (and optionally NCBI_EMAIL) in the environment to use the higher limit when resolving large batches.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
adaptiSeq ships a real, importable Python API. The three public functions return values and raise typed exceptions — they never call sys.exit and never print colour codes — so you can drive them from a script, notebook, or pipeline.

from adaptiseq import fetch, resolve, get_metadata

docs.title: get_metadata — parsed metadata rows
docs.text:
rows = get_metadata("SRR7706354")                 # list[dict] (TSV columns)
rows = get_metadata("CRR311377")                  # GSA -> list[dict] (CSV columns)
rows = get_metadata("SRR7706354", database="ena") # force a database

Writes the same *.metadata.* files the CLI writes; with no outdir it uses a temporary directory and cleans up.

docs.title: resolve — URLs without downloading
docs.text:
urls = resolve("SRR7706354", database="ena")      # list[str] of download URLs
urls = resolve("SRR7706354", gzip=True)            # the *.fastq.gz links

Fetches metadata, then returns the URLs the engine would fetch — useful for auditing or feeding another downloader.

docs.title: fetch — download and verify
docs.text:
# a single accession
result = fetch("SRR1553469", outdir="data/", gzip=True)

# a whole batch (same -i semantics as the CLI: a file of accessions)
result = fetch("accessions.txt", outdir="data/", gzip=True,
               jobs=20, adaptive=True, controller="topdown")

print(result.accession, result.outdir, result.failed)
print(result.success_ids, result.fail_ids)

fetch is a thin wrapper over the same pipeline the CLI runs. It returns a FetchResult:

Field Type Meaning accession str the input (accession or file path) outdir Path where files were written failed bool whether any Run ultimately failed success_ids list[str] Runs in success.log fail_ids list[str] Runs in fail.log

fetch accepts keyword equivalents of the CLI flags: metadata, gzip, fastq, threads, merge, database, parallel, aspera, speed, skip_md5, protocol, quiet, engine, segment_size_mb, max_segments, max_conns_per_host (0 = auto, jobs × max_segments), jobs, adaptive, controller ("topdown", "bottomup", "budget", "greedy" or "knee"; None = the default), probe_window, cc_penalty, meta_jobs and aspera_efficiency, plus an optional reporter to capture progress. --no-sra-fallback is a CLI flag only in 0.1.12; fetch always allows the fallback to NCBI SRA, which is announced through the reporter.

result.failed is True when any Run could not be delivered and verified (the CLI exits 1 in the same case), and result.fail_ids names them.

docs.title: Typed exceptions
docs.text:
All inherit from AdaptiSeqError (in adaptiseq.errors):

Exception Raised when InvalidAccessionError the accession matches no supported format MetadataError metadata could not be fetched / was empty everywhere DownloadError a file could not be resolved or downloaded IntegrityError a file failed md5 / vdb-validate after all retries MergeError a merge input was missing PreflightError a required external tool is missing from PATH EngineUnavailableError an unknown engine was requested 
from adaptiseq import fetch
from adaptiseq.errors import PreflightError, MetadataError

try:
    fetch("SRR1553469", outdir="data/", gzip=True)
except PreflightError as e:
    print("missing tool:", e.message, "->", e.solution)
except MetadataError as e:
    print("metadata problem:", e.message)

Note adaptiseq.resolve (the package attribute) is the public function; it shadows the internal resolve.py submodule, which is reached via importlib.import_module("adaptiseq.resolve").

docs.title: Type hints
docs.text: The package ships a py.typed marker, so type checkers see adaptiSeq's annotations.
